The reason for the former is this: because that which is subjectible, as such, is not predicable, as is self-evident; therefore, since a Logical Universal is predicable, the subjectible, as such, will not be a Logical universal. But since a metaphysical universal is situated neither in predicability nor in subjectibility, but in the inexistence of one thing in many, just as the subjectible, as such, can still be one thing apt to be in many, so too it will be able to be a metaphysical universal. The reason for the latter is because a Genus, which is subjectible (for example, animal with respect to living), is also predicable with respect to rational and irrational.

VII. Q. *Whether a Genus in general is predicated univocally of a Genus of real being and a Genus of a being of reason?* I answer. These two Genera, according to their material parts alone, agree with one another analogically; because Being can only be predicated analogically of real being and a being of reason. But if they are taken in the being of a genus, and as they are of Logical consideration; since the Logical artifice and concept of both are precisely the same, there is no doubt that they agree with one another univocally.

VIII. Q. *Since the highest Genus is as far removed from the lowest as the lowest Genus is from the Species; why is the lowest Genus a different universal than the species; and the highest Genus not different from the lowest genus?* I answer. That this diversity is not to be sought from the greater or lesser distance that universals have in the predicamental line; but from their quidditative concept. Since, therefore, both the highest Genus and the lowest Genus are predicated as a material part; while the species is predicated as the whole essence; there can be no doubt that the species differs more from the lowest Genus than the latter does from the highest.

IX. Q. *Whether the concept defining a designated Genus is the concept that formally makes an exercised Genus?* I answer. Since the concept making a Genus in the exercised act must also make a universal in the exercised act; and a universal cannot be made by a simple concept not abstracting from a multitude; and the concept defining a designated Genus does not abstract from a multitude; just as it is a simple concept, so it is not a concept making a Genus in the exercised act. Therefore, by the definition of a Genus, a Genus is defined as designated, but it is not made as exercised.

X. Q. *What is a species taken in general?* I answer. Although it is certain that a metaphysical species taken in general can rightly be called, *One thing apt to exist in many as the whole essence*; yet because there is a huge distinction between this and a Logical species, one might not undeservedly ask whether, since a Logical universal is predicable, a definition in general can be given for a Logical Species? <-*On the origin of Virtue.*->

**XL.** Virtue holds the property of being of divine origin <note>original: "(1)"</note>; for these three parts of it together constitute true virtue; and each of them is always found joined with the other two. And in effect, in prudence there is also fortitude, in that the mind, in searching for the truth, struggles and labors at it, nor does it rest until it finds it; there is also temperance, it being a wise thing to ignore certain things. In temperance, then, one finds prudence, which advises us not to neglect things useful to life, so as not to suffer detriment from them; and therefore Medicine is of divine origin, because dictated by this eternal truth: there is also fortitude, so that one may know how to keep oneself far from pleasures. Finally, in fortitude, there is also found prudence to defend the honest; there is then temperance, so that the victors do not wish to destroy the vanquished, whom they can without harm keep alive.

The target, sixteen fingers wide and of equal height, should be made of iron, firm and resembling an elephant. <note>verse 44</note>
One should bind these firmly between two branches of a pillar, at the height of a man's chest. <note>verse 45</note>
Having pierced through them and emerged on the other side, the arrow should strike the ground; in this manner, one should practice hitting with skill. <note>verse 46</note>
When the arrow is held by the index finger at the side of the thumb, and the bow is held in the grip, with the nock properly positioned, this is called level-aiming. <note>verse 47</note>
In level-aiming, the string is drawn below; therefore, drawing from above is called upward-aiming. <note>verse 48</note>
Downward-aiming is appropriate for a target located high above, while upward-aiming is for a target located low below; for a target at eye level, it should be level. <note>verse 49</note>
A target sixteen fingers in circumference is called a coarse target, while one two fingers wide is fine, and one five fingers wide is a head-target. <note>verse 50</note>
A target inferred by sound is called a transcendent target; thus, the five types of targets should be demonstrated in their piercing. <note>verse 51</note>
Moving horizontally, going forward, rotating, and jumping up; their locations are said to be in the sky, on the ground, or in water. <note>verse 52</note>
Two hundred units is said to be the best distance, one hundred and fifty is the medium, and one hundred and twenty is the minimum for practice on the ground. <note>verse 53</note>
One should strike the best distance with four arrows at a slow pace, using arrows that are straight, thick, fine, or leaf-less. <note>verse 54</note>
The king should demonstrate agility by shooting one arrow in the fall, one in the hand, and five in the sky, thus practicing hitting the target. <note>verse 55</note>

[M.] Are the angles equal or not? [D.] In no way. [M.] What if a figure made of three straight lines shows them as unequal? Can angles be equal in that case? [D.] They cannot be, by any means. [M.] You speak correctly. Tell me, I pray, which figure seems better and more beautiful to you? Is it the one made of equal lines, or the one that stands with unequal lines? [D.] Who doubts that the one in which equality prevails is better? [M.] Therefore, you prefer equality to inequality? [D.] I know not who would not prefer it. [M.] Let us look now at the figure which is perfect with three equal angles. What is in it regarding the three angles? That is, from the other side, it is positioned <note>the text describes the geometric completion of the triangle</note>. Is it a line or an angle? [D.] I see a line. [M.] What, therefore, if angle is added to angle and line to line? Do you not confess that equality is better in that figure in which this occurs? [D.] I confess it, indeed. [M.] I do not see at all how this is done with three lines. [D.] Can it be done with four lines? [M.] It certainly can. [D.] Is a figure that stands with four equal lines better than one that stands with three? [M.] Certainly it is better, for equality prevails more in it. [D.] What, therefore, do you think of this one that is formed with four equal straight lines? Do you think that all its angles can be equal, or do you not think so? [D.] I see that it is possible, M. [M.] In what way? [D.] If two are more obtuse and two are more acute, M. [M.] Namely, just as both are more obtuse and both are more acute to each other? [D.] Very truly and very aptly, M. [M.] Do you see how much equality can be held in <term>a</term> and <term>b</term>? [D.] I see it, indeed. [M.] It is impossible for it to be finished with four equal lines if not all angles, or at least two pairs of angles, are equal. [D.] I see it and hold it most firmly, M. [M.] Does nothing move you, even in these things, regarding such a great and hidden justice? [D.] In what way, M.? [M.] I will say that nothing, as I judge, is justice unless it is equality. But <term>aequitas</term> <gloss>equity/fairness</gloss> is called such from a certain equality, for what is equity in this virtue except that to each his own is attributed? Furthermore, to each his own cannot be attributed without some distinction, or do you think otherwise? [D.] It is manifest and I entirely agree, M. [M.] What need is there for distinction if all things are equal, so that nothing differs at all from another?

From this preceding point, it now becomes clear what simple things are and how they differ from mixed things; furthermore, that neither the forms nor the powers of the elements are abolished in a mixture, but are so modified and governed that, under the most free service of the mixture, they do not refuse to perform the duties entrusted to them and to conform their own actions to the nod of their empress form. It is further evident that a mixture is not composed merely of four elements. Finally, it is clear that it is a vain labor to derive all physical changes and generations from the varying temperament of those elements and their qualities. Therefore, let those dusty and trivial battles vanish, which Galen, Aristotle, Avicenna, Averroës, and others brought into the realm of natural philosophy. For if we pursue them too tediously and too curiously, they will bring about a greater loss of time, truth, and solid erudition than they will bring a victory over ignorance and falsity. Although those ancient founders of philosophy should not be held in contempt at once for some flaws, but rather should be deemed worthy of perennial glory, because they applied their midwifery hand and paternal care to receive philosophy as it wailed from the cradle, and to increase its strength toward a flourishing youth. Koertius undertook a study of that part of the <term>Cynegeticus</term> <gloss>On Hunting</gloss> which is called technical, but he was intercepted by death before he could bring it to a conclusion. He first explained that not only is the arrangement inconvenient, but the teaching itself is so incomplete and obscure that it could hardly be useful to hunters. It must be admitted that he argued this with justice, but it confirms our conjecture regarding the origin of this little book. For the heir of Xenophon, a man certainly not unacquainted with rhetorical studies but little skilled in writing, kept the series of facts intact, just as he had found them written out in the volume handed down to him, and did not dare to add anything from his own knowledge to the rules that might clarify them or arrange them in a suitable order.

But many of the precepts in this part of the work, Koertius says, are so false that they could in no way have been written by a man truly skilled in hunting. He was prevented by fate from explaining and establishing this opinion with a full number of examples. a little of that spark of life which animated, it is said, the pebbles of Pyrrha <note>According to Greek mythology, after the Great Flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulated the earth by throwing stones behind them, which turned into people.</note>, I would make it my duty to repeat to him what I have just told you about Thales."

I answered the man from Priene: "Mandraite, I conceive and I share your enthusiasm; it is only the fanaticism of virtue and truth that is not to be feared. Go! your story adds to the veneration I already held for the name of Thales. Your delirium is quite natural, and so is his. One does nothing great, one invents nothing sublime, if one does not have the measure of one's genius, and the feeling of one's strengths. Thales is right to be jealous of his discovery; it is his property; it belongs more to him than the conquests of Semiramis <note>A legendary queen of Babylon.</note> belonged to that woman. One must hold onto the good action one has been capable of, to a strong and bold thought that one has managed to produce. Modesty is the virtue of mediocrity. Why not do oneself justice, and claim it for oneself just as for others?"

We parted at Myus, a small Ionian town, halfway from Priene to Miletus. It is there that the Meander <note>A river in Asia Minor, known for its winding course.</note>, after so many detours, finally falls into the sea, and regrets not having made even more in such an agreeable region.

Fatigued by the weight of the heat, I went to take refuge in an old, half-open temple, because the <term>neocoros</term> <gloss>temple warden or caretaker</gloss> was cleaning it at that moment. In the back of the sanctuary, I made out, not without difficulty because of the lack of light, the seated statue of an old man, covered in a long, very dirty cloak. His shoulder was burdened with a dusty axe.
